newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. blames Iraq for delay in food deliveries.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blames Iraq for delay in food deliveries.

text.p: The United States on Thursday said that Iraq as well as the United Nations was to blame for the slow pace of food and medical deliveries under a humanitarian plan allowing Baghdad to sell some of its oil despite trade sanctions.
"Not all the bureaucratic delays are here in New York, there are bureaucratic delays in Iraq," said U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson.

A U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that Iraq had decided not to distribute any food until 30 days worth of items needed for its ration basket of goods was stocked in warehouses.
"They can't hand out a sandwich until there are 30 days supply ... it is not logical and it is one of the things slowing down distribution," he said.

At issue is a plan that allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of its crude oil over six months, mainly to purchase food and medicine as an exception to broad sanctions instituted in August 1990, after Iraq invaded Kuwait.

Iraq has been contracting to sell oil since the plan's start on Dec. 10 but no goods have yet arrived in the country, leading to charges and countercharges from all parties involved about who was to blame for the delay.

The Security Council reviewed a 90-day progress report on the deal's implementation on Thursday. Although the oil sales side of the deal was proceeding with little trouble, the report said aid deliveries were slower than expected.

Iraq has blamed the United States as well as the United Nations for the delay. On Wednesday, the United States lifted its objections to 13 contracts for soap and detergent, only after gaining assurances the shipments would be sufficiently monitored by U.N. observers on the ground.

France's U.N. envoy, Herve Ladsous, told the council that the first deliveries might not reach the Iraq people until May and said all had to speed up procedures. His timetable was not disputed by the U.S. official.

The United Nations on last Friday said that the first food shipments were due at the end of March, although they had been approved on Feb. 14. One vessel carrying 25,350 tons of wheat left France on Feb. 19 but had mechanical trouble and now will not arrive before March 30.

Part of the delays were attributed by U.N. officials to stringent procedures set up by the Security Council to make sure the goods shipped to Iraq fall under its guidelines and were monitored adequately.
In addition the United Nations had to make sure there was enough money deposited in a special escrow account from oil sales to pay suppliers.
